title: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill dies keeping the slab
summary: Oighrig nic Dhòmhnaill keeps the slab for the rest of her life, as the lot gave it her, and that rest is shorter than anyone at the clearing looked for: she dies in the keepers' house in the winter after the meeting of the cups, and the families ask that a new lot be drawn.

title: The lot falls to Gilleasbuig Beag
summary: The bag of pebbles is filled again and passed among the households near the crack. The white stone comes out in the hand of Gilleasbuig Beag, a broad, quiet man known for mending roofs and cutting hazel, who goes pale rather than glad at what his open hand shows.

title: A basket found under the bed-place
summary: A kinswoman of Gilleasbuig, in his house on another errand, lifts a cloth expecting food and finds a basket of broken coal from the vein, more than any hand is owed by the handful. She says nothing that day, but tells her husband before she sleeps, and within three days the near valley knows.

title: Gilleasbuig does not deny it
summary: Called to the clearing, Gilleasbuig Beag owns the basket at once and says he took the coal against a hard winter, for an old mother who sleeps cold, and for no other use. He asks, when the judgement is given, what the stone gains by the coal's return that his mother does not lose by going without it.

title: The families judge Gilleasbuig by silence
summary: The households argue long in the cold before an old woman of Cnoc chaol says what none of the near families will say first: that the vein was never any one hearth's to keep behind a cloth, however true the love that took it. The clearing's silence, held past any voice rising to answer it, stands as the judgement.

title: Gilleasbuig Beag rowed to Eilean chrom
summary: Three men of the near households row Gilleasbuig Beag out to Eilean chrom and put him ashore, then pull back to open water and leave him without a boat to return in. He is the first anyone remembers exiled for the vein.

title: A fire seen three nights on Eilean chrom
summary: The near coast watches a small fire on Eilean chrom's low rise the first night, smaller the second, and a coal's worth of red at dusk the third, gone before full dark. No fire is seen there again, and no boat is sent to learn why.

title: The basket set inside the keepers' house
summary: The kinswoman who found the coal carries the basket to the keepers' house at Tobar dhìreach and sets it under its cloth just inside the door. No household proposes burning it; it was not theirs to burn before Gilleasbuig took it, and the judgement has settled that it never will be.

title: The lot falls to Giorsal Bhàn
summary: A new lot is drawn from the same bag that gave the stone to Oighrig and then to Gilleasbuig, and this time it is Giorsal Bhàn's hand that opens on the white pebble. She closes her hand on it and says she will keep it, and moves into the keepers' house before the month is out.

title: Giorsal lays the coal back under the slab
summary: On a still morning near the year's turn, Giorsal Bhàn kneels at the slab's lower edge and presses the broken coal back into the gap between stone and earth, piece by piece, returning a second day to finish it, until the basket holds nothing at all.

title: "The coal went home"
summary: By the summer after Giorsal Bhàn empties the basket into the slab's edge, the four words are already going round the near valley as if they had always been there: that the coal went home. No one near the crack can afterward say who spoke them first.

title: Eilean chrom left to itself
summary: The island stands ungrazed and unfished through the years after Gilleasbuig Beag's exile. Children of the near coast are told not to ask about the island with the spring on it, and are given the same short answer when they ask anyway.

title: Calum Ciar comes to the clearing
summary: Calum Ciar, elder son of Eilidh Ghlas and eleventh to hold Dùn ìseal under the king, walks up the valley to the slab and asks that the next lot be drawn at Dùn ìseal in his own sight, so the hill may see the vein's lot drawn as honestly as the hill's own.

title: The families refuse Calum Ciar
summary: The households near the crack answer Calum Ciar with the same held silence they gave Gilleasbuig Beag: the lot has been drawn at the slab since the custom began and will go on being drawn there, in the sight of whoever near the crack cares to watch. Calum Ciar thanks them and does not argue it.

title: Calum Ciar puts the question to the king
summary: At the ford that summer, Calum Ciar carries the same question to the king. The king hears him without anger or haste and says only that the slab is older than the hill, and older than the grove of his own crowning, and that he will not overrule so old a thing for the asking of a man not two hundred years in the world.

title: The line between hill and slab holds unwritten
summary: Calum Ciar goes home from the ford and asks nothing more of it. The hill rules the grazing and calls the gatherings, answering to the king for both; the keepers rule the vein, answering to no one the telling can name. The line is sworn to in no words either side writes down, and it holds.
